https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/2.text: Crime Local government Darlington Darlington MP issues warning to illegal vape shop owners By Bill Edgar Local Democracy Reporter Share 0 Comments (Image: Stuart Boulton) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Darlington ’s MP has warned “criminals aren’t welcome in this town” as she vowed to campaign for tougher powers to shut down vape shops and rogue businesses. Labour MP Lola McEvoy has called for a licensing scheme for businesses selling vapes, saying councils need greater powers to know which businesses are operating. Her comments came after she joined council officials during a crackdown on illegal tobacco and vapes at three premises in Darlington. Ms McEvoy said she would lobby the Government for powers allowing councils to close problem businesses for up to 12 months. She said: “We need a licensing scheme for any business registering in the town. We need to know who’s in the town, what sort of business they are doing and who they are.” The MP said stronger links between agencies were also needed to tackle illegal tobacco sales and wider criminality. “We need to make sure we have joined-up working between the police and trading standards, who do brilliant jobs together here in Darlington but also the other bodies in the country,” she said. “We need to have an open conversation about the links between these, what are seen as low-level crimes like illegal cigarettes and the wider crime network in the country. “Criminals aren’t welcome in this town.” The crackdown comes as the Government moves towards giving councils greater control over new vape shops. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said retailers wanting to set up businesses selling e-cigarettes will need to seek permission from their local council under proposed changes to planning policy. He said the aim was to give communities “the power to turn things around” and clamp down on businesses causing harm while supporting those to help bring life back to high streets. Last month, three shops were ordered to close for three months after council raids . Illegal cigarettes and hand-rolling tobacco worth almost £3,000 were seized from an unlocked vehicle linked to Vape City on Bondgate, while more than £5,000 of illicit goods were seized from Cherry Berry on Parkgate, according to Darlington Borough Council. Closure notices were served on Red Market on Neasham Road, Romanian Shop on North Road and Vape City on Bondgate. Read more Council reveals what Darlington households can use to line new food waste caddy bins Decision on future of Darlington aesthetics clinic offering Botox and fillers delayed Locals to benefit from affordable homes at new Darlington garden village development The council said the action followed intelligence gathering into the supply of illegal vapes and cigarettes in Darlington, including their alleged sale to children. A fourth premises, Pick & Pay on North Road, was also handed a three-month closure order earlier this month . Normal retail shops, including those selling cigarettes, currently do not need a specific licence to open and trade and current national legislation does not allow permanent closure of premises. Magistrates can impose an initial closure order of up to three months, with a further three-month extension available if required. https://english.radio.cz/czechs-mark-58-.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Czechs mark 58 years since Soviet-led invasion Facebook Twitter Czechs are marking the 58th anniversary of the invasion of Czechoslovakia by Soviet-led Warsaw Pact troops that crushed the Prague Spring reform movement in 1968. The invasion began overnight on August 21, 1968 and dozens of Czechoslovak citizens were killed in the first hours of the invasion alone, either in clashes with the troops or in traffic accidents caused by the occupying forces. Commemorative events honoring their memory are taking place around the country. In Prague one of the main events was held outside Czech Radio’s headquarters on Vinohradska street where some of the worst clashes with the invaders took place. Addressing the gathering, President Pavel stressed the importance of public-service media both in August 1968 and today, when, he said, there is once again pressure to restrict them. Senate Speaker Miloš Vystrčil, echoed those sentiments, saying that Independent media and courage are among the first targets of those in power, who want to impose “normalization” and bring society under control. He called for courage and urged people not to “bend their spines.” The speeches of Chamber of Deputies Speaker Tomio Okamura and Finance Minister Alena Schillerová, who represented the ruling parties, were met with booing and chants of “shame”, reflecting anger over the government’s plan to abolish license fees and replace them with state funds. Many fear this would leave the public broadcasters vulnerable to political pressure. Cultural events marking the anniversary in Prague include the NeverMore 68 festival at Prague's Exhibition Grounds and a Music Against Forgetting event in the lower part of Wenceslas Square. BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — Hungary ordered 10 members of Russia’s diplomatic mission in Budapest to leave the country over activities deemed unacceptable, the government said Tuesday, signaling a shift away from the previous administration's warm relations with Moscow. Log in here » BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — Hungary ordered 10 members of Russia’s diplomatic mission in Budapest to leave the country over activities deemed unacceptable, the government said Tuesday, signaling a shift away from the previous administration’s warm relations with Moscow. The Russian ambassador was informed that “according to the assessment of the Hungarian authorities, 10 members of the Russian mission had engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention,” Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said. That is a reference to an international treaty that governs the conduct of diplomats. Russia said that it planned to respond. FILE - Russia's ambassador to Hungary, Evgeny Stanislavov, is surrounded by media as he leaves the Hungarian Foreign Ministry building, in Budapest, Thursday, May 14, 2026. (AP Photo, File) The expulsions come months after Hungary’s Prime Minister Peter Magyar was sworn in on a promise to tackle corruption and dismantle the power structures left behind by his predecessor Viktor Orbán, who governed the European Union country for 16 years. Orbán, who is not related to the foreign minister, was an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin who repeatedly delayed or blocked EU sanctions on Russia and pursued energy deals with Russia. The foreign minister didn’t specify the alleged activities or say how long the Russian personnel had to leave Hungary, but stressed that her country seeks to maintain diplomatic contacts with Moscow. “This decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty,” Orbán wrote in a statement. “It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules.” The Russian Foreign Ministry, in comments to Russia’s state news agency RIA Novosti, vowed to provide “an appropriate response” to the expulsions. It didn’t elaborate. European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said Tuesday that “we take note of Hungary’s legitimate decision” to expel the Russian diplomats. He said it was an expected reaction due to “Russia’s persistent campaign in using hybrid attacks against the EU and its member states.” European leaders have repeatedly accused Moscow of conducting vast “hybrid warfare” campaigns against their countries, a litany of allegations that have included sabotage, election interference and an attempted attack at a German airport. On Tuesday, Romanian authorities said they had detained a 40-year-old Russian citizen suspected of spying for Moscow between February and July this year, allegedly with a view to carrying out acts of sabotage after collecting “information of a military nature.” Romania’s anti-organized crime agency, DIICOT, said the suspect took and sent photos of Romanian and NATO equipment and the movement of military personnel in several counties that “endangered national security.” The Romanian intelligence service, SRI, said the Russian citizen had been instructed by an intermediary to take photos and videos “with targets of strategic military interest, including Ukrainian ANTONOV cargo aircraft,” while they were on Romanian territory. The SRI added the case indicated a “similar pattern to that used on the territory of European states by networks of saboteurs” coordinated by Russia. Moldovan police also said Tuesday that a 49-year-old man, originally from Azerbaijan, had been detained on allegations of collecting information for Russian intelligence services. Police said he was targeting military targets in the country and some U.S. facilities in Moldova, and that the information he collected was to be sent to a person believed to be from Russian special services. Police said the suspect was allegedly “trained to carry out diversionary activities” in Ukraine and Moldova. He has been placed in pre-trial detention for 30 days. Russia has repeatedly denied allegations that it is trying to destabilize countries throughout Europe. ——— McGrath reported from Leamington Spa, England. Associated Press journalists Vanessa Gera in Warsaw, Poland and Sam McNeil in Brussels contributed. https://www.leicestermercury.co.uk/news/.text: News Inside the 'fairytale' town with rainbow buildings just over a one-hour flight from Midlands airport Originally a medieval fishing port, it has been named one of the world's most picturesque small towns nottinghampost Bookmark Share Comments News By Ben Lyons Content Editor Amy Jones 06:00, 11 OCT 2026 Bookmark Kinsale has been named as one of the world's most beautiful towns (Image: Getty Images) Get the latest Leicestershire Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. More info Join us on WhatsApp While Britain boasts plenty of picturesque towns, occasionally it pays to venture slightly further afield to discover locations that feel plucked straight from a fairytale. Characterised by vividly coloured buildings lining meandering cobbled lanes, one particular destination has even been likened to a film set, with its acclaimed restaurants and fresh seafood catches further cementing its irresistible charm. With a population hovering just below 6,000, the delightful town of Kinsale has consistently attracted attention, lauded for its stunning vistas and thriving culinary landscape. Originally a medieval fishing port, the town boasts considerable heritage, featuring a picturesque harbour where boats gently bob on the water. It also claims the honour of representing the southern endpoint of the 2,500km Wild Atlantic Way, the magnificent coastal trail that winds down from the Inishowen Peninsula in the north to Kinsale in County Cork. Access is straightforward, with flights departing from several UK airports to Cork, including Birmingham, lasting just an hour and 15 minutes, followed by a brief journey by car to Kinsale. This year, Kinsale was recognised as one of the world's most picturesque small towns by Condé Nast Traveller, cementing its long-held status as Ireland's most vibrant settlement. The town draws crowds who come to wander its winding, cobbled streets, lined with eye-catching Georgian buildings painted in pink, orange, green, blue and yellow hues, while enjoying the diverse selection of shops, pubs, eateries and cottages that justify its international reputation, reports the Express . Colourful storefronts Adding to its fairytale character, the multi-coloured townhouses showcase delightful hanging baskets and flower arrangements, enhanced by classic cast-iron street lighting and distinctive red benches. The area has garnered recognition as a compact yet accessible town providing plentiful shopping experiences, from Foley's Gift Shop and Bookstór to various jewellery outlets, such as Kinsale Silver and Stone Mad, reports the Irish Mirror. It's been hailed as the most colourful town in Ireland (Image: Getty Images) The delightful red-and-white frontage of The Collector coffeehouse is bound to attract guests, along with Cosy Café and sweet shop Koko Kinsale. However, this only begins to reveal the town's culinary offerings, which feature outstanding restaurants and quality seafood venues, reinforcing its standing as the 'Gourmet Capital of Ireland'. Flourishing food culture A standout attraction is the Michelin-starred Bastion, located in the heart of the town and run by Paul McDonald with his wife, Helen. The restaurant features Irish-influenced dishes and locally caught seafood prepared with a modern, creative flair that "brings depth in their flavours and textures", as noted by the Michelin Guide . Besides this culinary gem, visitors are spoilt for choice when it comes to places to eat across the town, with more than 60 thriving restaurants, cafés, and gastropubs - a food scene that's truly exceptional. Celebrating its distinguished reputation for fine dining, Kinsale also stages several events, including its annual Gourmet Festival and Street Feast, alongside a dedicated Restaurant Week. 'Beautiful and unique' However, its charm and picture-perfect scenery mean Kinsale can often become overrun with tourists. One local commented on Reddit: "Kinsale is the beaten path. It's basically Disneyland for tourists. If you want off the beaten path, go to somewhere like Rathkeale in County Limerick or Dunmanway." Yet, it's hard to resist visiting the vibrant town that one traveller compared to a Wes Anderson film set, the director known for movies such as The Grand Budapest Hotel and Moonrise Kingdom. Many others continue to praise the town that has firmly established itself as a must-visit destination. The colourful streets of Kinsale in County Cork are packed with shops and restaurants (Image: Getty Images) "Kinsale is definitely worth a stop. Cute town, lots of shopping, good eats, a small beach and two interesting historical forts/ruins nearby," one visitor remarked. A further traveller enthused: "Kinsale is excellent! Make sure you stop in The Spaniard and Bulmans for a pint. Cobh is a good little day trip from there if you have time." A third visitor simply noted: "Kinsale is beautiful and quite unique", while another declared: "We loved Kinsale. It's cute, colourful, walkable, and Ireland's self-proclaimed culinary capital." They suggested embarking on a walking tour from the Kinsale Tourist Information Centre, pointing out that the town is ideally situated near Cork, Cobh, and Blarney Castle — making it an ideal base for those looking to extend their stay beyond Ireland's most picturesque town. Photograph: Google Earth View image in fullscreen The combined storage at Menindee Lakes has fallen below 480 gigalitres for the first time since 2021. Photograph: Google Earth Murray-Darling Basin Menindee Lakes water levels drop to lowest in five years as experts warn of mass fish deaths NSW government imposes water restrictions after Menindee water volumes fall below 2021 levels Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Water levels at Menindee Lakes in western New South Wales have fallen to their lowest point in five years, prompting the state government to impose upstream water use restrictions as experts warn of potential mass fish deaths over summer. Combined storage at Menindee Lakes fell below 480 gigalitres earlier this month, the first time since 2021. In the upper Menindee Lakes, water volumes have dropped below 250GL, a level that triggers temporary state water restrictions across parts of the northern Murray-Darling basin. Mass fish deaths feared as Minns government promise to restore Murray-Darling rivers in doubt Read more The restrictions limit access for some irrigators and are intended to preserve water for critical human needs and the environment. It follows periods of low rainfall in the catchment throughout the past 12 months, with experts warning of a growing risk of summer fish kills unless flows down to Menindee Lakes via the Darling-Baaka River improve. Menindee was the site of catastrophic fish kills in 2018, 2019 and 2023, which saw millions of dead fish wash up along stretches of the Darling-Baaka. “Government officials are predicting with a level of certainty that unless there’s more water flowing into the Baaka-Darling River that there will be fish kills at Menindee this summer,” said Prof Jamie Pittock of the Australian National University and the Wentworth Group of Concerned Scientists. “We need a major rainfall event to happen and for the state governments to prevent irrigators from pumping out the first flush of water.” Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter Graeme McCrabb, who was one of the first Menindee residents to raise the alarm about the 2018-19 disasters, said the combined Menindee Lakes had reached “drought reserve volumes”. He said this effectively meant conservation of water “at all costs”. McCrabb said he was hopeful that recent rainfall in Queensland may result in some replenishment of the Menindee system. “There are some small inflows coming across the Queensland border now which probably give us some hope for the summer. But we would need more on top of that,” he said. “If we don’t get inflows, the risk [of fish kills] would be very high in January or February.” He said a milder summer would also lower the risk. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When he publishes Sign up to Clear Air Australia Adam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisis after newsletter promotion “I’m worried about fish kills to be honest,” McCrabb said. “It’s a tough time or sad time when the water starts to get that real green algal look.” Days after winning the 2023 state election, the premier, Chris Minns, and senior state ministers visited Menindee and committed to an investigation of the mass fish kills . An expert panel was established under the northern basin connectivity program , which recommended limiting upstream overextraction during dry periods, to help maintain flows in tributaries into the Darling-Baaka River to Menindee Lakes. This was to try to reduce the risk of catastrophes such as fish kills and large-scale drying. The panel delivered its final report two years ago but the state government is yet to implement it. McCrabb said he was disappointed the government had not followed through on the recommendations of the connectivity panel. “Since the fish kills, government agencies have made no policy changes to improve water quality outcomes,” he said. Comment has been sought from the NSW water minister, Rose Jackson. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: An 1817 painting by Nicolas-André Monsiau shows the French naval officer Jean-François de Galaup (the count of Pérouse), left, receiving orders for a round-the-world mission from Louis XVI. Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/Alamy View image in fullscreen An 1817 painting by Nicolas-André Monsiau shows the French naval officer Jean-François de Galaup (the count of Pérouse), left, receiving orders for a round-the-world mission from Louis XVI. Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/Alamy France Rare love letters to French aristocrat shed light on Louis XVI maritime mystery ‘Miracle’ cache of letters written by French scientist who died in ill-fated La Pérouse mission give personal account of 1785 voyage Kim Willsher in Paris Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 08.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google As he prepared to climb the scaffolding to be publicly executed by guillotine on 21 January 1793, Louis XVI is reported to have asked: “Is there news of Monsieur de la Pérouse?” He was referring to Jean-François de Galaup, the count of Pérouse , a naval officer and navigator whom the French king had dispatched in 1785 on a round-the-world scientific mission to rival discoveries made by the English explorer Captain James Cook. View image in fullscreen The veiled love letters sent by Jean-André Mongez to Louise Victoire Le Cloustier were discovered in a book of engravings. Photograph: Daguerre Paris The two ships under La Pérouse’s command, La Boussole and L’Astrolabe, disappeared three years later after leaving Botany Bay in Australia. The wrecks were only formally identified in 2005 and exactly what happened to them remains a mystery to this day. Now rare letters written by an illustrious scientist who perished in 1788 have resurfaced, giving a new and personal account of the voyage. They are described as veiled love letters addressed to the married daughter of an aristocratic family, and were discovered hidden in a book of engravings being examined in preparation for auction. Ludovic Miran, a book and manuscript expert for the auctioneers selling the letters next month, described the find as “a miracle”. “We have a certain number of documents from the expedition but they are almost all scientific, so these personal letters are extremely rare,” Miran told the Guardian. “They throw a completely new light on what is in France an extraordinary scientific and historical event.” The La Pérouse expedition was launched at a time when Britain and France were in a period of intense rivalry over colonial expansion. La Pérouse was a great admirer of Cook and his maritime mapping and scientific discoveries, but Louis XVI had more political and trade ambitions. The French wanted to create trade routes and discover whether the secret information they had that Britain was planning to establish a permanent base at Botany Bay, giving it access to unexplored areas of the Pacific region, was correct. La Pérouse’s ships, carrying 225 crew, officers and scientists, sailed from Brest on France’s Atlantic coast on 1 August 1785 and for almost three years sent reports during stopovers including from Alaska, California, Asia, Russia and Samoa, where the captain of the Astrolabe and 11 men were killed. At the time of Louis XVI’s execution, there had been no news of the frigates since their departure from Botany Bay in March 1788. To La Pérouse’s dismay, Captain Arthur Phillip and Britain’s First Fleet had beaten him to the Australian coast – inhabited by an Indigenous population for tens of thousands of years – by just six days. View image in fullscreen A map of the voyage taken by La Boussole and L’Astrolabe, an expedition commissioned by Louis XVI. Photograph: Daguerre Paris La Boussole and L’Astrolabe are believed to have foundered on coral reefs at Vanikoro east of the Solomon Islands during a tornado a few months later. Wreckage was discovered in 1826 and 1964 but only formally identified in 2005. The letters were written by Jean-André Mongez, a brilliant scientist, director of an illustrious science revue and church canon who was with the expedition, to Louise Victoire Le Cloustier, the daughter of a minor noble family from Rouen, Normandy. Miran said Mongez used the letters to express his unhappiness at her marriage and appears to repent for previous bad behaviour. “He writes several times: ‘I will be back, I will be another man, a better man’,” Miran said. “One has the impression he has not behaved well towards her and she has put him in his place.” View image in fullscreen Captain Arthur Phillip raises a British flag at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788. Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty This may, he added, have been behind Mongez’s decision to undertake such a long and perilous journey. “The references are often veiled, but they seem to have had a very close relationship but he seems to have caused some offence at some point. They are intimate, very personal letters,” he said. “He tells her he is leaving ‘a bit for the love of fame and the desire to acquire new knowledge’, but he already had scientific glory and a good career and they would have all read James Cook’s works before leaving so they knew about the dangers. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion “We will never know why he decided to join this perilous journey, but it is clear he was leaving in part because of this emotional relationship.” Miran added: “The correspondence also provides answers as to how these young men endured three years of navigation around the world, a completely new and unimaginable experience. We learn how they withstood the shock of such a crazy journey and horrible conditions. “He recounts how his friend and others were massacred on one stop. In his last letter he tells her the expedition has taken a sad turn and he now only wants to come home because such unhappiness is not compensated for by the meagre scientific results they have. “Perhaps it is a journey of redemption.” View image in fullscreen The letters, valued at €30,000-€50,000, are being sold at auction in Paris. Photograph: Daguerre Paris Le Cloustier died in 1821, like the rest of the world unaware of the fate of Mongez or the expedition. “But she kept the letters and we can tell they have been read, and reread. I would imagine she had to hide them from her husband,” Miran said. The auctioneer Benoît Derouineau said he had discovered the letters in an “unremarkable” 19th-century book of engravings being prepared for sale. “I didn’t realise what they were at first. They had clearly been carefully saved and hidden. Perhaps because they were a kind of love letter and the recipient didn’t want them seen. But she hadn’t thrown them away or burned them,” he said. “That Louis XVI is said to have asked about La Pérouse shows how much was invested in this expedition. It was a very important event in France.” The letters, valued at €30,000-€50,000, are being sold as one lot by Daguerre at the Hôtel Drouot, Paris, on 17 November.
